children: New Delhi, Sept. 23 -- The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the finance ministry have asked banks to ensure adequate cash availability at ATMs from 15 October as a cautionary measure, when new charges on select UPI transactions take effect, according to two people aware of the matter.
"The use of cash through ATMs may see a temporary increase as people and merchants adjust to the new Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) regime for certain UPI transactions,'' the people said.

A 0.4% MDR will apply to specified person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above Rs.2,000, subject to a maximum charge of Rs.300 for transactions of Rs.75,000 and above. Person-to-person transactions will remain free, as will P2M transactions up to Rs.2,000. Earlier, Mint reported that the finance ministry will monitor daily UPI transactions.

The potential shift towards cash may come as banks' ATM networks have contracted over the years, even as digital payments continue to expand. The government and RBI are therefore monitoring whether the introduction of charges on select UPI transactions could trigger a temporary increase in cash withdrawals, according to the people cited above.

"Unfortunately, the decision to charge for UPI is a step towards disincentivising digital payments and incentivising cash in a price-sensitive market," said Aruna Sharma, former member of the Reserve Bank of India's High-level Committee on Deepening the Digital Payments in India.
Queries emailed to the RBI, finance ministry and 12 public sector banks remained unanswered at the time of publication.
About 96% of P2M UPI transaction volume is below Rs.2,000 and will therefore remain outside the standard MDR regime, according to the government's framework.

"If fear of a shift to cash goes viral because of this step, it's not just withdrawals. Merchants will also deposit cash, and accounting charges will shoot up, triggering a cash economy," Sharma said. She added that ATMs may need to be reconfigured to handle higher demand, including potentially through the return of higher-denomination currency.
The possibility of a temporary cash response is significant because the physical infrastructure supporting cash withdrawals has itself been shrinking.
RBI data show that the total number of ATMs, including machines deployed by white-label ATM operators, declined to 251,057 at the end of March 2025 from 253,417 a year earlier.

The decline was driven mainly by the closure of off-site machines, even as on-site ATMs increased. Public sector banks had 133,544 ATMs at the end of March 2025, down from 134,694 a year earlier, while private-sector banks reduced their network to 77,117 from 79,884. White-label ATM operators, in contrast, increased their network to 36,216 from 34,602.

Across scheduled commercial banks and white-label operators, off-site ATMs declined to 119,734 at the end of March 2025 from 127,301 a year earlier, while on-site ATMs increased to 131,323 from 126,116.

The trend is also visible in ATM cash withdrawals. RBI payment-system data show debit-card ATM cash withdrawals at about 68,975 lakh transactions in FY23. By FY26, the volume had fallen to about 53,394 lakh transactions, while the value of ATM cash withdrawals declined from roughly Rs.32.8 lakh crore to around Rs.28.5 trillion.
At the same time, the broader cash trend complicates the assumption that digital payments necessarily displace banknotes.

Currency in circulation stood at Rs.42.86 trillion at the end of August 2026, up 12.5% from a year earlier. At the end of March 2026, currency in circulation stood at about Rs.41.66 trillion, while the value of banknotes in circulation was about Rs.41.24 trillion.

The rise in cash has occurred alongside rapid growth in digital payments. UPI transactions reached 2,451 crore in August, with the value of transactions at about Rs.29.82 trillion, according to NPCI data.

"Temporarily, a certain surge will be there. People's corresponding actions will also be towards using cash for some time. So naturally, instead of going to the bank branch, they will start going to the ATM again. To that extent, it can increase," said Prodosh Ganguly, a former senior RBI official.

Ganguly said the increase would not necessarily signal a reversal of the longer-term shift towards digital payments, as consumers have already developed a habit of using digital modes for everyday transactions, including small-value payments.

Charan Singh, chief executive officer and founding director of EGROW Foundation and former non-executive chairman of Punjab & Sind Bank, said the preparedness of the government, RBI and banking industry was appropriate given the possibility of initial implementation-related disruptions.

"I think the preparation by the Central Government, the Reserve Bank, and banking industry is good public policy. To be prepared for different scenarios is worth appreciating. There could be hiccups in the early stages of implementation. This preparation will ensure that there is confidence maintained in the currency and banking system of the country,'' Singh said.

title: RBI, FinMin ask banks to ensure ATM cash ahead of UPI charges
